title: Spacecraft Touches Down on Mysterious Mercury: New Discoveries Unveiled by Newser
body:
The joint European Space Agency‑Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency mission BepiColombo has successfully entered orbit around Mercury, becoming only the second spacecraft ever to circle the innermost planet after NASA’s MESSENGER probe. The achievement marks a milestone for planetary science, opening a new window onto a world that remains largely mysterious despite its proximity to Earth. Engineers and scientists now have an unprecedented platform to study Mercury’s extreme environment, its magnetic field, and clues to the early Solar System.

BepiColombo, a twin‑craft system launched in October 2018, comprises the Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO) built by ESA and the Mio (Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter) constructed by JAXA. After a seven‑year odyssey that included three gravity‑assist fly‑bys of Earth, Venus and Mercury itself, the MPO performed a delicate insertion burn on 5 October, slowing enough to be captured by the planet’s weak gravity. The maneuver, executed from a distance of roughly 200 km above the surface, required the spacecraft’s 2.5‑tonne main engine to fire for nearly three minutes, a feat made more challenging by Mercury’s intense solar radiation and the need to conserve fuel for the mission’s multi‑year science campaign.

“Mercury is the terrestrial planet we know the least about,” said Geraint Jones, project scientist for BepiColombo at the European Space Agency. “Its proximity to the Sun makes it a natural laboratory for studying planetary formation, core dynamics, and space weather.” Unlike Earth, Mercury’s iron‑rich core occupies a disproportionately large fraction of its volume, generating a magnetic field that is about 1% as strong as Earth’s but surprisingly complex. BepiColombo’s suite of instruments—including a magnetometer, a spectrometer for surface composition, and a laser altimeter—will map the planet’s magnetic topology, examine the distribution of volatile elements, and measure the topography with unprecedented precision.

The mission arrives at a time when comparative planetology is gaining renewed emphasis. Data from MESSENGER, which orbited Mercury from 2011 to 2015, revealed a surface scarred by giant impact basins, a surprising abundance of sulfur, and evidence of past volcanic activity. However, many questions remain unresolved: Why does Mercury’s magnetic field exhibit a north‑south asymmetry? How did its thin exosphere, composed of atoms stripped from the surface by solar wind, evolve over billions of years? And what does Mercury’s composition tell us about the building blocks of the inner Solar System? BepiColombo’s dual‑orbit design—MPO in a low, near‑circular orbit and Mio in a highly elliptical trajectory—allows simultaneous observation of the planet’s surface and its magnetosphere, offering a holistic view that previous missions could not achieve.

Technical challenges have been formidable. The spacecraft must endure temperature swings from -180 °C to over 400 °C within each Mercury day, necessitating a sophisticated sunshield and a thermal control system that can adapt in real time. Moreover, the intense solar flux—more than ten times that at Earth—pressurizes the spacecraft’s power and communications subsystems. Engineers have mitigated these risks through extensive testing and by employing a high‑gain antenna that can transmit data back to Earth despite the Sun’s interference. The first science data, expected to begin streaming in the coming weeks, will be relayed through ESA’s deep‑space network and JAXA’s ground stations, providing a steady flow of high‑resolution images and measurements.

Looking ahead, BepiColombo is slated to conduct a primary science phase lasting at least one Earth year, during which it will complete a global mapping of Mercury’s surface and magnetic field. The mission’s findings could reshape our understanding of planetary differentiation and the role of solar proximity in shaping planetary atmospheres. As the spacecraft continues its delicate dance around the Sun‑kissed world, the international team behind BepiColombo anticipates that the data will not only fill long‑standing gaps about Mercury but also inform future exploration of exoplanets that orbit close to their stars. The successful orbital insertion is thus not merely a technical triumph; it is the opening act of a scientific saga that promises to illuminate the origins of our own planet and the broader cosmos.
